source.title: Revisiting Training Scale: An Empirical Study of Token Count, Power Consumption, and Parameter Efficiency

record.tranche_reason: Measures post-training evaluation loss-derived inverse perplexity across training-token conditions for a fixed model, bearing on the token-count aspect of loss scaling, but does not fit or evaluate a power law.
record.gate_note: The study reports energy-aware parameter-efficiency and GPU-power results, but these do not measure the loss-scaling or compute-optimal-allocation claims. Only its explicit statement about inverse-perplexity variation is recorded as a result relevant to V1.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version. It fine-tunes an already-pretrained TinyLlama 1.1B Chat model on 500K–2M TinyStories tokens (lr 1e-6, 3 epochs). Its outcome is an energy-aware efficiency metric that divides by token count, so the decline is largely built in. The only loss-related statement is that inverse perplexity 'varied only modestly', with no per-condition values. That measure is a prompt-based evaluation loss after fine-tuning, not held-out pretraining loss, over a 4x range with no power-law fit. It cannot bear on V1, and only loosely on V5 (fine-tuning) or V7. Scaling laws appear only in the related-work discussion.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that more training tokens under fixed conditions systematically reduce energy-aware parameter efficiency and raise power use, while inverse perplexity changes only modestly. They present this as reinforcing diminishing returns in neural scaling and call for energy-aware evaluation of token budgets. They also describe the study as a confirmatory replication of their own dissertation.
record.recipe_differences: This is an energy-aware token-count efficiency study, not a power-law fitting or compute-optimal scaling experiment; it uses one model and three token conditions.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies token count; no sensitivity analysis of scaling-law fitting choices is reported.

fits_no_version.finding: Energy-aware parameter efficiency (inverse perplexity divided by tokens, parameters and RMS power) declines monotonically from 500K to 2M fine-tuning tokens (F(2,98)=24,268, ηg²=.997). RMS GPU power rises with token count. The efficiency decline is largely mechanical, since tokens are in the denominator.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-token, per-watt efficiency of small-scale fine-tuning falls as token count grows under fixed hardware and epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-fine-tuning inverse perplexity changes only modestly across 500K, 1M and 2M tokens. No values are reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning a pretrained 1.1B model on 4x more TinyStories tokens at lr 1e-6 yields small evaluation-loss changes.

record.problems: Only one model architecture and GPU class are used. The token range is limited, and no power-law fit or condition-specific inverse-perplexity values are reported. Evaluation sometimes used fallback prompts or a valid training batch when prompt-based evaluation was unstable.
record.rows_left_out: Efficiency and power-consumption results are not rows because they do not measure a claim version's loss-scaling or allocation behavior.

untested.parts: All of it: no pretraining runs, no parameter or compute variation, no power-law fit, no multi-order-of-magnitude range.
Fine-tuning token scaling is touched only qualitatively, with no loss values or fitted form.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/tests classification and its V1 limits_scope label are dropped. The study measures no pretraining loss scaling, and its single loss statement has no numbers. The 'training' here is fine-tuning an already-pretrained chat model at a tiny learning rate with batch size 1 and sequence length 64. Evaluation uses fallback prompts or a training batch when unstable, which makes the loss signal unreliable. The efficiency metric's monotonic decline follows largely from dividing by tokens processed.

versions.untested_parts: Tests only the token-count dimension on one model and a 500K–2M token range; it does not fit a power law or test parameter-count or compute scaling, nor establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit or prediction of larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or optimization of parameter and token counts.
No comparison of architectures or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modalities or training regimes are evaluated.
No downstream-task performance is evaluated or related to pretraining loss.
No fitted exponents, fitting choices, or departures from fitted power-law curves are assessed.

rows.subject: TinyLlama 1.1B Chat v1.0
rows.operation_detail: Varied training-token count and measured post-training evaluation loss as inverse perplexity.
rows.measure: Post-training inverse perplexity, computed from evaluation loss
rows.value: Inverse perplexity varied only modestly across token conditions; condition-specific values are not stated.
rows.note: The reported statement is an aggregate across the three token conditions. It does not specify whether the loss-derived measure follows a power law.
rows.check: The subject is a pretrained chat model fine-tuned on TinyStories, not a pretraining run. The measure is evaluation loss on a default or fallback prompt, sometimes on a training batch, not held-out pretraining loss. The range covers only 500K–2M tokens and no per-condition values are given. It does not measure what V1 names, and the values can't be read for V5.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The study reports only modest inverse-perplexity variation over this narrow token range and does not fit a power law; r1 therefore limits what can be concluded about the stated scaling law.
